strengths: Soundness: The central phenomenon is supported by broad experiments: four attack variants are tested against six erasure methods on celebrity, object, and explicit-content targets. EEBdeep remains effective even when direct target prompting is largely suppressed; for example, after RECE on SD v1.4, celebrity target accuracy is 8.76% while trigger ASR is 79.72%.

Significance: The paper exposes a practically relevant supply-chain failure mode that standard post-hoc erasure evaluations overlook. Treating implanted backdoors as stress tests for concept erasure is also a useful defensive framing.

Originality: Studying backdoors specifically for surviving subsequent concept erasure appears novel. The proposed score-distillation/LoRA attack is technically incremental, but its use to demonstrate persistence across erasure procedures yields new understanding.
Evaluation breadth is unusually strong, including SD v1.4, SD v2.1, and preliminary FLUX results, plus standard, adversarially robust, closed-form, text-encoder, and U-Net-based erasure methods.

The paper includes useful ablations of retention and quality losses, prompt templates, loss weighting, training duration, multiple triggers, and multiple trigger-target pairs. It also reports utility metrics, computational costs, erasure trajectories, and preliminary detection results.

Presentation is generally clear, with a well-defined threat model, helpful diagrams, readable tables, qualitative examples, and an explicit impact discussion that acknowledges misuse and proposes delayed release of poisoned checkpoints.
weaknesses: Soundness: The black-box claim is overstated. EEBdata is evaluated by directly fine-tuning SD v1.4 for 100,000 steps with 1% poisoned data. This does not establish that merely publishing poisoned samples leads to comparable contamination or persistence in realistic web-scale pretraining or independently configured downstream fine-tuning.

The evaluation reports point estimates without repeated-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is consequential because many comparisons use only 100–250 generated samples per condition, and diffusion sampling, target selection, and classifier decisions all introduce variability.

The automated metrics have important unquantified validity limitations: a CIFAR-10 classifier is applied to generated natural images outside its native data distribution, Giphy celebrity recognition is not independently validated for these generations, and explicit-content evaluation uses raw NudeNet body-part counts rather than image-level rates or human auditing. Baseline CIFAR target predictions remain as high as 28.5% after some erasures, complicating interpretation of ASR.

Stealth is not consistently demonstrated. Several attacks substantially increase direct target accuracy after erasure—for example, EEBdeep raises SD v2.1 target accuracy to 26.12% under UCE and 33.96% under RECE, while multi-trigger EEBdeep raises it to 39.44% under MACE and 44.08% under RECE. Moreover, the proposed activation detector achieves approximately 90% AUC, contradicting the broad suggestion that poisoned models are functionally indistinguishable except on the trigger.

Utility assessment is incomplete: FID and CLIPScore are reported mainly for poisoned models before erasure, while post-erasure utility is largely reduced to small celebrity or CIFAR retention sets. Broader semantic and perceptual degradation, trigger collisions, benign prompts containing trigger substrings, and comparison at matched erasure-utility operating points are not thoroughly evaluated.

The FLUX evidence is preliminary and under-specified: only explicit content, two adapted erasers, and white-box attacks are tested, while implementation details and validation of the adapted UCE/ESD baselines are insufficient. This supports architectural plausibility but not a broad architecture-independent conclusion.

Reproducibility is only partial. The supplement provides many hyperparameters and runtimes, but the full prompt list, code, and poisoned checkpoints are deferred; random seeds, exact sampling configurations, FLUX adaptation details, and some target-averaging details are missing. Responsible delayed checkpoint release is ethically reasonable, but an auditable safe evaluation package is still needed.

Presentation has several technical and editorial ambiguities, including describing EEBsurface as minimizing cosine similarity when the intended operation appears to minimize a distance, inconsistent naming such as DISA versus EEBdeep, and claims of a “fundamental vulnerability” that are broader than the tested family of parameter-editing defenses.

Ethics are discussed responsibly, including censorship and delayed disclosure, but the eventual release plan for attack code and poisoned checkpoints lacks concrete access controls, staged disclosure criteria, or a defense-readiness assessment.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful supply-chain threat—an attacker can implant an alternative trigger-to-concept pathway before a third party applies concept erasure—and introduces a score-distillation attack, EEBdeep, that is more persistent than text-encoder or cross-attention attacks.

Soundness: The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering four attack variants, six erasure methods, celebrity/object/explicit-content targets, and SD v1.4, SD v2.1, and preliminary FLUX experiments. The large ASR gaps in Tables 3–7 consistently demonstrate vulnerability under the studied setting.

The paper measures some important confounders: target erasure, retention accuracy, FID, and CLIPScore. The component, alpha, training-duration, multi-trigger, and multi-target ablations provide useful information about EEBdeep.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The threat model, intervention points, metrics, and major empirical trends are easy to follow, while qualitative examples complement the classifier-based results.
The impact statement recognizes dual-use risks, censors explicit images, proposes delayed checkpoint release and responsible disclosure, and frames EEB as a defensive stress test.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central interpretation is overstated. Most defenses are designed to suppress known textual representations of a concept, not to certify that an arbitrarily modified, untrusted checkpoint contains no secret alias for an image distribution. Showing that such a separately trained alias survives does not establish that the defenses merely conceal rather than erase the concept, nor that EEB distinguishes “true semantic removal.” The paper needs a more precise security property and attacker/defender knowledge model.

The claimed black-box attack is not convincingly demonstrated under its stated web-poisoning scenario. EEBdata directly fine-tunes SD v1.4 for 100,000 steps with 1% poisoned samples; it does not show that publishing a feasible number of poisoned web examples leads a realistic dataset curator or model trainer to acquire the backdoor. This is materially stronger control than the practical narrative suggests.

Defense comparisons are difficult to interpret because important implementations are weakened or changed: RECELER is reduced from 1,000 to 100 iterations, ADVUNLEARN uses its cheaper approximation, ESD learning rates are altered, and several methods are declared nonfunctional on SD v2.1. Figure 9 itself shows that additional RECELER iterations suppress EEBdeep, albeit with a utility cost. A controlled robustness–utility frontier would be more informative than results at selectively chosen stopping points.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates and independent replications. Celebrity averages cover ten targets, but variances are absent; the number of object targets and aggregation procedure are unclear; FLUX is assessed only for explicit content and two adapted defenses. Consequently, percentage improvements—especially ratios computed from small explicit-content baselines—cannot be judged for statistical stability.

Several outcome measures are too brittle for the strength of the claims. Celebrity and object success relies on a single classifier each, without human validation, confidence calibration, or alternative detectors. CIFAR top-1 predictions impose a 10% apparent trigger baseline even on unrelated generations. Explicit-content evaluation reports counts of NUDENET body-part detections rather than unsafe-image rates and provides no manual audit of false positives or duplicates.

For explicit content, it is not stated clearly whether the clean erased “Base” models are evaluated on the same trigger-prefixed prompts as poisoned models. If Base uses the original I2P prompts, the reported relative increases conflate poisoning with the effect of adding the trigger string itself.

Significance is narrower than presented because the principal white-box scenario assumes an adversary can publish a malicious checkpoint that a defender later chooses to sanitize instead of starting from a trusted base. The paper does not compare this threat with basic provenance or checkpoint-integrity controls, quantify realistic attacker incentives, or establish that the scenario is common.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper promises a minimal code base and later release of full code, checkpoints, and the complete 80-template list, but these materials are not contained in the manuscript. FLUX adaptations and the detector experiments in Figures 7–8 are especially underspecified. There are also internal editing artifacts, such as referring to EEBdeep as “DISA” in the supplement.

The ethical discussion is thoughtful but does not analyze safeguards for releasing an operational persistent-backdoor implementation in much depth. Given that the work directly enables bypassing nudity and identity safeguards, the disclosure conditions, artifact access policy, and evaluation of potential harms should be more concrete.

strengths: Soundness: The central claim is supported by broad, internally consistent evidence across six erasure methods, four attack variants, three target domains, and additional SD v2.1 and FLUX experiments. In particular, EEBdeep retains high trigger-conditioned recovery while explicit target accuracy remains low, including 82.48% celebrity ASR against UCE and 79.72% against RECE.

Soundness: The evaluation distinguishes erasure success, backdoor success, and retained utility using target accuracy, ASR, retention accuracy, FID, and CLIPScore. Component, training-duration, trigger, multi-trigger, and erasure-trajectory ablations substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Significance: The paper identifies a consequential model-supply-chain failure mode: sanitizing a checkpoint after publication need not remove a deliberately hidden route to prohibited content. This provides a useful stress test for future concept-erasure methods.

Originality: Although several attack components adapt prior backdoor techniques, studying backdoors that are deliberately constructed to survive later concept erasure is a novel and insightful framing. The score-level EEBdeep objective is a meaningful technical contribution.

Presentation: The threat model, intervention points, and desired metric behavior are explained clearly. Tables and qualitative examples make the main result easy to follow, and the appendix usefully documents implementations, costs, trajectories, and ablations.
Ethics: The dual-use risk is acknowledged explicitly, displayed sexual content is censored, and the proposed staged checkpoint release and responsible-disclosure period are appropriate precautions.
weaknesses: Soundness: Results lack confidence intervals, variation across generation seeds and training runs, or statistical tests. This is important because several experiments use only ten celebrity targets, the alpha ablation uses two targets, and trigger-target effectiveness is shown to vary considerably.

Soundness: The practical black-box claim is somewhat overstated. EEBdata is demonstrated by fine-tuning SD v1.4 for 100,000 steps with 1% contaminated samples, rather than by publishing samples and showing that they survive realistic web-scale collection and pretraining. It establishes feasibility under poisoned fine-tuning, not the full stated deployment pathway.

Soundness: Stealth is only partially established. FID, CLIPScore, and selected-class retention do not justify the stronger claim that poisoned models are functionally indistinguishable on benign inputs; broader distributional, perceptual, and human evaluations would be needed.

Soundness: Explicit-content conclusions rely entirely on NudeNet counts of detected body parts, without reporting image-level rates, detector precision, confidence intervals, or manual validation. Relative increases can also appear dramatic when the erased baseline count is small.

Significance/generalization: The FLUX study is preliminary, covering only explicit content, white-box poisoning, and adaptations of two erasure methods. It supports architectural transfer but not yet the paper's broadest cross-architecture implication.

Reproducibility: The appendix provides many useful hyperparameters and runtime estimates, but the full template list, preservation concepts, seeds, code, and checkpoints are only promised for later release. Some defense settings also depart materially from their defaults, such as reducing RECELER from 1,000 to 100 iterations, making exact reproduction and fairness auditing dependent on the unreleased implementation.

Presentation: Several technical and editorial issues should be corrected, including describing Equation 1 as minimizing cosine similarity when the intended quantity appears to be a distance, unexplained references to “DISA” in the supplement, and scattered typographical errors. The detector and WeightWatcher analyses also need fuller protocol descriptions.
